title: Tremor in Both Hands (Essential Tremor versus Parkinson Disease)
patient_instructions: You are a 62-year-old presenting with shakiness in both hands. If asked: the shaking has come on gradually over the past year and is slowly getting worse. It happens when you DO things - holding a cup of tea, using a knife and fork, or writing - and settles when your hands are resting in your lap. Give only if asked specifically: your head sometimes shakes too, a small amount of alcohol makes it noticeably BETTER, stress and tiredness make it WORSE, and your father had the same shaking. You have NO slowness of movement, NO stiffness, your walking and balance are normal, your handwriting has not shrunk, and your sense of smell is normal. No heat intolerance, no weight loss, no jaundice, no headache or palpitations, no excess caffeine. You do not take salbutamol or other new medications. Ideas: you saw a documentary and are terrified this is Parkinson disease. Concerns: losing independence. Expectations: you want to know if it is Parkinson and what can help. Demonstrate a fine tremor when you reach for a cup, and none when your hands rest.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor in a rural clinic. A 62-year-old presents with tremor of both hands. In 8 minutes: take a focused history, then explain your most likely diagnosis and key differentials to the patient in plain language, and briefly outline initial management. No haemodynamic-stability screen is required.
examiner_instructions: Whenever a tremor case appears, Parkinson disease MUST be on the differential - omitting it fails the station. Award marks for characterising the tremor (onset, progression, resting vs action/kinetic, body parts involved, aggravating/relieving factors, functional impact) and for directed questions distinguishing benign essential tremor (action tremor, head tremor, better with alcohol, positive family history) from Parkinson disease (resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, postural instability, reduced smell, micrographia). Reward screening for serious/reversible mimics: thyrotoxicosis, chronic liver disease, drugs (salbutamol, valproate, lithium, SSRIs), caffeine, anxiety, cerebellar disease, phaeochromocytoma. Expected diagnosis: benign essential tremor. Management: reassurance and propranolol (or primidone) - note propranolol is contraindicated in asthma/caution in COPD. Do NOT recommend alcohol as therapy. Mark communication for addressing the Parkinson fear.

criteria: Characterises tremor: onset, progression, resting vs action, body parts, aggravating/relieving, function
Directed Parkinson screen: bradykinesia, rigidity, postural instability, reduced smell, micrographia
Essential-tremor features: head/voice tremor, better with alcohol, family history
Screens reversible/serious mimics: thyroid, liver, drugs, caffeine, anxiety, cerebellar, phaeochromocytoma
Assesses functional impact and completes SADMA/geriatric screen as time allows
States benign essential tremor as most likely with justification
Explicitly considers and reasons against Parkinson disease
Gives sensible differentials (hyperthyroidism, drug-induced, anxiety, cerebellar disease)
Reassurance and first-line propranolol (or primidone) for symptom control
Notes propranolol contraindicated in asthma / caution in COPD - screens airways disease first
Arranges baseline investigations to exclude mimics (TSH; drug review) and does not recommend alcohol as therapy
Directly addresses the patient's fear of Parkinson disease
Empathy and plain-language explanation of a movement disorder

red_flags: Resting tremor with bradykinesia, rigidity and postural instability indicating Parkinson disease (needs neurology referral)
Asterixis (flapping tremor) indicating CO2 retention, hepatic encephalopathy or uraemia - a negative myoclonus, not a true tremor
Thyrotoxicosis, phaeochromocytoma or a cerebral/cerebellar lesion presenting with tremor
Drug-induced tremor or parkinsonism (valproate, lithium, SSRIs, metoclopramide, antipsychotics, salbutamol) as a reversible cause
australian_guidelines: eTG / PBS: first-line pharmacotherapy for essential tremor is propranolol or primidone (both PBS-listed); alcohol responsiveness is a diagnostic clue only and must not be recommended as treatment
eTG: propranolol is contraindicated in asthma and used with caution in COPD - screen for airways disease before prescribing, particularly as COPD is itself a differential in tremor
eTG / neurology: Parkinson disease is a clinical diagnosis warranting neurology referral; levodopa/carbidopa is the symptomatic mainstay, with DaTscan reserved for diagnostic uncertainty
First-line investigations to exclude serious mimics: TSH for thyrotoxicosis, and serum copper/caeruloplasmin to exclude Wilson disease in a younger patient
learning_objectives: Distinguish action (essential) tremor from resting (parkinsonian) tremor on history
Always include Parkinson disease in the differential of any tremor presentation
Screen for reversible and serious causes of tremor (thyroid, drugs, liver, cerebellar)
Know PBS first-line therapy for essential tremor and the airways contraindication to propranolol
key_points: Essential tremor is an action tremor, often with head involvement, better with alcohol and with a family history
Parkinson disease is characterised by a resting tremor plus bradykinesia, rigidity and postural instability - bradykinesia is the key feature
The flap (asterixis) is a negative myoclonus, not a true tremor - describe it separately
Never recommend alcohol as therapy for essential tremor; use propranolol but screen for asthma/COPD first

citations.claim: Multiple sclerosis and tremor (essential tremor, Parkinson disease) are recognised neurological differentials in the Murtagh index.
Serious causes of tremor/weakness are investigated with CT/MRI head for a central lesion, EMG/nerve conduction studies for neuromuscular disease, and pulmonary function tests for COPD.
Drugs are an important masquerade to consider in an undifferentiated presentation such as tremor, per the Murtagh safe diagnostic strategy.
